channel.title: Chatbot on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Chatbot on Best of AI

item.title: Baidu ERNIE
item.description:
ERNIE, which stands for Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration, is Baidu’s answer to ChatGPT. The consumer chatbot answers questions, writes and edits text, generates images, and handles tasks in Chinese and other languages, and it is built into Baidu’s search engine and apps. It benefits from Baidu’s knowledge graph and search data, and is a major option for Chinese-language users.

For developers and companies, Baidu offers ERNIE models through its Qianfan cloud platform, with APIs, fine-tuning, and tools for building AI applications. The company has released versions of its models with open weights, which lets developers run them independently. The models support multimodal inputs and reasoning, and are used in enterprise products, cloud services, and Baidu’s autonomous driving and other businesses.

item.title: Bland AI
item.description:
Bland provides voice agents that talk on real phone calls. Companies use them to answer inbound calls, call leads, confirm appointments, and run surveys, replacing or supplementing call center staff. The agents speak naturally, handle interruptions, and can work around the clock.

Developers control behavior through a system of Conversational Pathways, which define the steps and branches of a call, along with tools to call APIs, look up records, and update systems. The platform supports many languages and voices, call analytics, and handoff to human agents. It offers APIs for scaling to large volumes of calls.

item.title: Cresta
item.description:
Cresta works with customer service and sales teams. During a live call or chat, it analyzes the conversation and gives an agent real-time guidance, such as the next best response, a reminder to cover a compliance point, or a prompt to offer a relevant product. New agents ramp faster, and experienced ones get support on tough conversations.

After calls, Cresta scores interactions automatically against quality criteria, replacing the small samples that supervisors normally review. Managers see which behaviors drive better outcomes and can coach agents using real examples. Analytics surface trends in why customers call and where processes break down.

item.title: Decagon
item.description:
Decagon builds AI agents for customer service. Companies connect it to their help center, policies, and internal systems, and the agent answers questions, looks up orders, processes refunds, and handles account changes. It aims to resolve the issue instead of only deflecting people to articles.

A key idea is that support teams control the agent without engineers. They write instructions in natural language, called Agent Operating Procedures, that define how to handle scenarios, which keeps the behavior consistent and reviewable. Testing and monitoring tools show how the agent performs, and analytics highlight why customers contact support.

item.title: Help Scout
item.description:
Help Scout is for teams that want customer support without a heavy ticketing feel. Messages arrive in shared inboxes, where agents can assign conversations, leave private notes, and collaborate, while customers get replies that look like ordinary emails. That personal feel is a selling point for businesses that value relationships.

The product includes a knowledge base called Docs, a chat and messaging widget called Beacon, and reports on response times and satisfaction. Workflows automate routing and tagging. AI features draft replies from past conversations and help articles, summarize long threads, and adjust tone, and an AI answers questions for customers using the knowledge base.

item.title: Kore.ai
item.description:
Kore.ai helps large organizations deploy virtual assistants. Companies design conversations and workflows in a low-code environment, connect them to back-end systems, and publish them on websites, mobile apps, messaging platforms, and voice lines. The assistants can answer questions and complete tasks such as resetting a password or checking a balance.

The platform has moved from rule-based dialogue to generative AI and agents. It supports large language models from several providers, retrieval over company content, and tools for building multi-agent systems, with governance features for testing and monitoring. Prebuilt solutions for banking, healthcare, retail, and HR speed up projects, and agent assist tools support human staff on live calls.

item.title: LivePerson
item.description:
LivePerson began with live chat and developed into a conversational platform. Brands use it to let customers message them on the channels they already use, with a mix of human agents and automated assistants. The platform manages the conversations, routes them to the right team, and records the data.

AI is central. Bots handle common requests, such as order status or billing questions, and hand off to agents when needed, and agent assist tools suggest responses. The company offers tools for building and managing assistants powered by large language models, with guardrails and analytics to check quality and compliance. Customers include banks, telecoms, and retailers.

item.title: Nomi
item.description:
Nomi lets users build a personal AI companion. You choose a name, appearance, personality traits, and backstory, then chat by text or voice. The app emphasizes memory, so the character recalls details you shared in earlier conversations and builds a continuing relationship, which is what many users value about it.

Relationship type is configurable, and group chats and shared experiences add variety. Users can see the companion’s interests and send images, and the creators have promoted the idea of an emotionally rich AI that grows with the user. The app runs on mobile and web.

item.title: Planhat
item.description:
Planhat is a customer platform built for subscription businesses. It connects to a company’s tools and data, builds a profile for each account, and shows health, usage trends, revenue, and conversations in one place. Teams use it to prepare for renewals and spot upsell opportunities.

Automation and workflows trigger tasks and outreach when something changes, such as a drop in usage or an upcoming renewal. Dashboards and reports show retention and growth, and AI summarizes accounts and suggests actions.

item.title: Retell AI
item.description:
Retell provides the infrastructure for voice agents. A developer defines an agent’s prompt and tools, connects a phone number, and the platform handles speech recognition, the language model, speech synthesis, and call control with natural turn-taking and interruption handling.

Use cases include answering customer calls, scheduling appointments, qualifying leads, and following up with customers. Integrations with calendars and CRMs let agents take actions, and analytics show call outcomes. Handoff to humans is supported.

item.title: Sierra
item.description:
Sierra focuses on replacing scripted chatbots with agents that can actually resolve customer issues. Companies such as consumer brands and subscription services deploy Sierra agents to answer questions, process returns, change plans, schedule appointments, and handle other tasks by connecting to back-end systems. The agent follows the company’s policies and tone, and hands off to a human when needed.

Several elements distinguish its approach. An Agent OS provides the tools for building, testing, and monitoring agents, with simulation and evaluation to catch problems before customers see them, and supports voice and messaging channels. The company often uses outcome-based pricing, where customers pay for resolved conversations instead of seats, which aligns cost with value. It combines multiple language models to improve reliability.

item.title: Synthflow
item.description:
Synthflow is a no-code voice agent platform. A user designs the call flow in a visual editor, picks a voice, connects a phone number, and the agent handles calls, such as answering questions, booking appointments, and qualifying leads. Integrations connect calendars and CRMs.

Agencies resell the platform with white-label options, building agents for dental offices, home services, and similar businesses. Analytics show call outcomes and transcripts.

Synthflow is paid, with plans by minutes. Voice agents need testing for accuracy and disclosure of AI use. Alternatives include Retell AI, Vapi, Bland AI, Air AI, and PolyAI. Synthflow suits agencies and small businesses deploying voice agents.

item.title: Taromi
item.description:
Taromi pairs the practice of tarot with AI interpretation. A user poses a question, draws cards from a virtual deck, and receives a written reading that explains the cards in context. Many users treat it as a prompt for reflection more than a prediction.

The format is easy to use daily, with options for different spreads and for saving past readings. Like horoscopes, tarot has no proven ability to foretell events, and readings generated by AI are creative text, not guidance backed by evidence.

item.title: Canary Technologies
item.description:
Canary builds software for hotels. Guests can check in online before arrival, sign registration forms, verify identity, and pay deposits, which shortens lines at the front desk. After arrival, messaging lets them ask for towels, late checkout, or recommendations through text instead of calling.

An AI layer answers common questions and handles requests, routing issues to staff when needed. Upsell tools offer room upgrades and add-ons at the right moment, which brings extra revenue. Other products cover contactless payments, digital tipping, and a guest-facing digital tablet in rooms.

item.title: Duve
item.description:
Duve is a guest experience platform. Before arrival, guests receive a digital check-in flow, can upload documents, and see offers for upgrades and extras. During the stay, a messaging assistant answers questions about the property and the area, and requests are routed to staff when a person is needed.

The platform includes a digital guidebook, upsell tools that present add-ons at the right moment, and integration with property management systems. For hoteliers and vacation rental managers, this reduces repetitive messages and brings extra revenue per booking.

item.title: GPT-6 Luna
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Luna on September 22, 2026, as the budget sibling to GPT-6 Sol. It shares Sol’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit but costs far less to run, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, making it OpenAI’s pick for high-volume tasks like classification, summarization, and routine chat where the heavier reasoning of GPT-6 Astra or Sol isn’t needed.

item.title: Grok 4.7
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026, alongside Grok Build, a terminal-native coding agent built around it. The model keeps the same per-token pricing as Grok 4.6 and offers a 500,000 token context window. Grok 5 is still in training at xAI with no committed release date, making 4.7 an interim update aimed mostly at coding and knowledge-work tasks.

item.title: Moveworks
item.description:
Moveworks brings an assistant to employee support. Workers ask for help in Slack, Teams, or a portal, and the system understands the request, finds the answer in company knowledge, or completes the action by connecting to IT and HR systems. Common examples are unlocking an account, requesting software, or finding a policy.

The company grew by focusing on large enterprises and on language understanding specific to workplace requests. It added generative AI and agent capabilities, with a platform for building custom agents and connecting to many business systems.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: Google CC
item.description:
CC acts like a morning assistant. Each day it sends an email, called Your Day Ahead, that pulls together calendar events, important messages, bills, and documents relevant to the day. You reply to the email to ask for changes, such as adding an event or digging into a topic, and CC acts on it.

It connects to a user’s Gmail, Calendar, and Drive and can also use the web for context. Because it works through email, there is no new app to learn. Google has expanded the experiment to support shared use by members of a household, with each person connecting their own accounts.

item.title: Zetik
item.description:
Zetik is a personal research assistant. A user picks topics, and the system monitors many source types, ranks what matters, and delivers a concise brief, so they stay informed without scanning feeds. It aims to surface signal across places that are hard to follow manually.

This suits founders, investors, and researchers who track fast-moving fields. Summaries need to link back to sources, and personalization improves as the tool learns what the user finds relevant.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: DeepSeek Chat
item.description:
DeepSeek Chat offers consumer access to DeepSeek’s language models. Users ask questions, draft text, write code, and work through math and logic, and a mode shows the model’s step-by-step reasoning before it gives an answer. It supports uploading files and searching the web.

DeepSeek drew wide attention when its models matched strong Western systems at much lower reported training cost, and it released the model weights openly, which let others run and study them. The chat app was one of the most downloaded in many countries soon after it launched.

item.title: Elastic AI Assistant
item.description:
Elastic AI Assistant is built into the Elastic stack, which many companies use for search, logs, and security monitoring. Users ask questions in plain language, such as what caused a spike in errors or what an alert means, and the assistant queries the data, explains findings, and suggests next steps.

For security teams, it helps triage alerts, write queries, and summarize incidents using the organization’s own data. For observability, it assists with investigating logs and metrics. Retrieval from indexed content grounds answers in real information, and administrators choose which language model provider to connect.

item.title: Gemini Pro
item.description: Gemini Pro refers to the mid-sized models in Google’s Gemini family, positioned between the smaller, cheaper Flash models and the heaviest reasoning options. Google’s naming moves with each generation, but the idea stays the same: Pro is the version intended for demanding everyday work without the cost or delay of the very largest model. Gemini was designed from the start to take in several types of input at once, so the same model reads text, looks at images, listens to audio, and watches video rather than handing those jobs to separate systems.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: Qwen Studio
item.description:
Qwen Studio is the consumer-facing way to use Alibaba’s Qwen models. Users chat with the assistant, search the web, upload documents and images for analysis, write code, and generate pictures and video. A mode shows the model’s reasoning for harder problems.

The Qwen family is notable for open-weight releases that developers can download and run, so Qwen Studio doubles as a showcase of what those models can do. It supports many languages, with strong coverage of Chinese and English.

item.title: BlenderBot 3
item.description: BlenderBot 3 is an open-domain chatbot that Meta AI released in August 2022, built on top of Meta’s own OPT-175B language model and fine-tuned to hold conversations, search the web for current information, and remember details across sessions. At 175 billion parameters it was, at the time, the largest publicly released conversational AI model, and Meta made the code, model card, and training data available alongside it, in contrast to closed systems like OpenAI’s models. It was designed to keep improving from real conversations: Meta let members of the public chat with it and collected feedback to retrain and refine it over time, along with safety filters meant to catch toxic or unsafe responses. Full access to the 175B model was restricted to approved researchers, though smaller 3B and 30B versions were released more openly through Meta’s ParlAI framework. It was a research project rather than a commercial product, and its public demo was later shut down; today it’s mostly of historical interest as one of the last major “research chatbot” releases before ChatGPT reset expectations for what a conversational model should do.

item.title: ChurnZero
item.description:
ChurnZero is built for customer success teams at software-as-a-service companies. It pulls in product usage data, support tickets, and CRM information to give each account a health score, so a team can see which customers are thriving and which are at risk of leaving before a renewal conversation turns bad.

Automation handles routine outreach. Playbooks trigger tasks and emails when a customer hits a milestone or goes quiet, in-app messages guide users inside the product, and dashboards track renewals, adoption, and revenue. AI features summarize accounts, draft messages, and suggest next actions, and a customer-facing portal can share progress with clients.

item.title: Kommunicate
item.description:
Kommunicate combines a chatbot builder with a shared inbox for agents. Businesses add a chat widget to their site or app, train a bot on help articles and FAQs, and let it answer routine questions, handing the conversation to a person when the bot cannot help or the customer asks.

The platform supports generative AI models and connects to knowledge bases, so answers draw on company content. Multi-channel support extends to messaging apps, and analytics show deflection rates and satisfaction. Integrations with CRMs and helpdesks keep data in sync.

item.title: Landbot
item.description:
Landbot lets non-developers design conversations visually. A user drags blocks onto a canvas to ask questions, branch based on answers, and connect to other tools, then publishes the flow on a website, a landing page, or WhatsApp. The conversational format often gets more responses than a plain form.

AI features add the ability to answer free-text questions from a knowledge base and to build flows from a description. Integrations send leads to CRMs and spreadsheets, and handoff routes complex chats to human agents. Templates cover lead generation, support, and onboarding.

item.title: Totango
item.description:
Totango helps subscription companies keep customers. It gathers usage and account data, scores health, and triggers playbooks when customers need attention. Modules called SuccessBLOCs package best-practice workflows that teams can adopt and adjust.

The company merged with Catalyst, another customer success platform, and the combined product serves teams from startups to enterprises. AI features summarize accounts and draft communications, and analytics show retention and expansion.

Totango has had a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Gainsight, ChurnZero, Planhat, Vitally, and HubSpot. Totango suits customer success teams at software companies.

item.title: Yellow.ai
item.description:
Yellow.ai builds AI agents for customer and employee service. A company connects it to systems such as CRMs and ticketing, trains it on content, and deploys across websites, messaging apps, and phone lines. The agents answer questions and complete tasks in many languages.

The platform emphasizes multilingual support, strong in markets such as India, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Tools for building, testing, and monitoring agents, along with analytics, support operations teams. Handoff to human agents is built in.

item.title: Ada
item.description: Ada helps companies handle customer support questions without adding staff. Its AI agent answers inquiries on websites, in apps, and over messaging channels by drawing on a company’s knowledge base and systems, and it can take actions such as checking an order, changing an address, or processing a return by connecting to back-end tools. When a request is too complex or sensitive, it hands the conversation to a human agent with context.

item.title: Balto
item.description:
Balto sits beside an agent during a call. The software listens to the conversation, recognizes where it is in a script or process, and shows prompts on the agent’s screen: a question to ask, a compliance statement to read, a way to answer an objection. The aim is consistent performance across a team and less reliance on memory.

Supervisors benefit as well. Balto scores calls automatically, shows which behaviors lead to better outcomes, and reduces the number of calls reviewers must listen to by hand. New agents can ramp faster because the software coaches them in real time. Industries with strict rules, such as insurance and financial services, use it for compliance.

item.title: Brave Leo
item.description: Leo sits in the browser’s sidebar and works with whatever page you are viewing. You can ask it to summarize an article or a long video transcript, explain a technical passage, extract key points from a PDF, or answer questions about the content, without copying text into a separate chatbot. It can also help write or rewrite text, translate, brainstorm, and answer general questions, with the option of using the web for current information.

item.title: Capacity
item.description:
Capacity aims to be a single assistant across several support functions. It connects to a company’s knowledge sources and systems, then answers questions from employees about IT, HR, and policies, and from customers about products and orders. Automated workflows can complete actions such as resetting a password or opening a ticket.

The pitch is reducing the volume of tickets that require a person. By resolving common requests automatically and escalating the rest with context, it can free staff for harder issues. Analytics show which questions come up most and where documentation is lacking.

item.title: Chatbase
item.description: Chatbase started as a simple way to create a chatbot from your own data. You upload files, point it to a website, or connect sources such as Notion, and it builds an agent that answers questions using that information. You embed the chat widget on your site with a snippet of code and you have support available around the clock. The simplicity made it popular with small businesses and startups that wanted a support bot without engineering work.

item.title: ChatGPT
item.description: ChatGPT is a chat interface to OpenAI’s language models. You type or speak a request and it answers in plain language, whether that means drafting an email, explaining a concept, debugging a function, or summarizing a long PDF. It can take images and files as input and generate images in return. For many people it is the first AI tool they ever used, and that familiarity is a big part of why it remains the default comparison for every other assistant.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Forethought AI
item.description: Forethought applies AI to the work that fills support queues. It reads incoming tickets and classifies them by topic and urgency, routes them to the right team, and drafts answers for human agents using the company’s knowledge base and past tickets. For common questions, its AI agents answer directly in chat and email and take simple actions such as checking an order status, handing off to a person when they cannot resolve the issue.

item.title: Freshdesk
item.description: Freshdesk gives support teams a single place to handle customer requests. Messages from email, a web form, live chat, phone, and channels like WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram land in a shared inbox as tickets that can be assigned, tagged, prioritized, and tracked against service-level targets. A knowledge base lets customers find answers on their own, and a customer portal shows the status of their requests. It is used by companies from small startups to large support organizations.

item.title: Gemini
item.description: Gemini is Google’s family of AI models and the assistant built on top of them. You can use it in the standalone Gemini app and website, but it also shows up inside the products many people already use: it can help draft emails in Gmail, rewrite text in Docs, summarize files in Drive, and answer questions on Android phones. If most of your work and personal life already runs on a Google account, that integration is the main reason to choose Gemini over another assistant.

item.title: Gemini Advanced
item.description:
Gemini Advanced was Google’s answer to ChatGPT Plus. When Google rebranded Bard as Gemini, it introduced Advanced as a subscription, sold through Google One, that gave access to its strongest model, longer conversations, and features like file uploads and integration with Gmail and Docs. It also bundled extra Google One storage, which made it attractive to people already paying for cloud storage.

Google later reorganized the plans. Gemini Advanced’s features moved into Google AI Pro, and a higher tier called Google AI Ultra provides the most advanced models, agent features, and generous limits for heavy users. The plans include perks such as video generation, deeper research tools, and integrations with Workspace apps, and the exact lineup changes with each product update.

item.title: Gladly
item.description:
Gladly organizes support around the customer, not the ticket. Instead of separate cases for each channel, all interactions with a person appear in a single timeline, so an agent sees the entire history when a customer reaches out. That makes support feel more personal and reduces repeating information.

Sidekick is the AI part. It answers common questions, completes tasks like order lookups, and hands off to a human with context when needed. Assistive features summarize history and suggest replies. Gladly is used by consumer brands that care about the quality of service.

item.title: Google Assistant
item.description: Google Assistant is the voice assistant that ships on Android phones, Nest speakers and displays, Android Auto, Wear OS watches, and many third-party smart home devices. You wake it with a phrase or a button, then ask it to set a timer, add a calendar event, send a message, play music, or turn off the lights. It works well for short, concrete commands, and a large ecosystem of smart home brands supports it, which made it one of the more capable options for controlling a connected home.

item.title: Gorgias
item.description:
Gorgias is a helpdesk made for online stores. Messages from email, live chat, social media, SMS, and phone arrive in one inbox, with the customer’s order history, shipping status, and account details shown next to the conversation. Agents can refund an order, edit an address, or cancel a shipment without leaving the ticket, which speeds up the most common support tasks in retail.

Automation takes care of a lot of the repetitive work. Rules route and tag tickets, macros fill in standard replies with order data, and self-service flows let shoppers track orders or request returns. An AI agent answers questions about shipping, returns, and products using the store’s policies and catalog, and can complete actions in the store before passing complex issues to people. Gorgias can also support sales conversations and product recommendations.

item.title: Helpshift
item.description:
Helpshift places support inside the app. Users reach help from a screen in a game or mobile product, without leaving to email, and conversations carry context about the device, account, and recent activity. Agents see this information and respond in the same thread.

AI reduces the load. Intent detection reads messages, classifies the issue, and routes it to the right team, while chatbots answer common questions and collect details before a human steps in. A knowledge base and automation tools support self-service, and analytics track satisfaction and resolution times.

item.title: Intercom
item.description:
Intercom began as a live chat widget for websites and now covers the full range of customer communication. It combines a messenger on your site or app, a shared inbox for support teams, a searchable help center, email, and product tours. Companies use it to answer questions, onboard new users, and keep conversations in one thread across channels. It is common among software and subscription businesses.

Fin is the AI agent at the center of the current product. It reads your help articles and past conversations, then answers customer questions directly in chat and email, including follow-ups. When it cannot solve a problem or the customer asks for a person, it hands the conversation to a human with context attached. Fin can also take actions in other systems, like checking an order or updating an account, if you connect it. A copilot for human agents drafts replies and summarizes long threads.

item.title: Kimi
item.description:
Kimi first gained attention for handling very long documents. Users can upload large PDFs, books, or collections of files and ask questions, and the assistant keeps track of the whole text, which suited tasks like summarizing reports and analyzing contracts. It also searches the web, writes and reasons about code, and has agent features that carry out multi-step tasks.

Moonshot AI releases powerful models, including open-weight versions of its Kimi K2 family, which are among the larger open models and strong at coding and agentic tasks. Developers use them through Moonshot’s API or run them through third-party providers, and they are often used inside coding tools. The company competes with other Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Zhipu.

item.title: Kustomer AI
item.description:
Kustomer takes a CRM-style approach to support. Instead of treating each ticket as an isolated item, it builds a timeline for each customer that includes every conversation, order, and interaction across channels. Agents see the full history in one view, which reduces the need to ask customers to repeat themselves. Channels include email, chat, SMS, social messaging, and voice, and workflow rules automate routing and tagging.

AI features have grown in importance. AI agents can answer common questions, check order status, and complete simple actions, escalating complex cases to humans with context. Tools for human agents summarize long histories, suggest replies, and classify issues, and insights analyze conversation patterns to find problems in products or processes. The system connects with e-commerce and business platforms to bring in order and account data.

item.title: Le Chat
item.description:
Le Chat is Mistral’s answer to ChatGPT and Claude. The French company designed the app for general use: answering questions, writing and editing, summarizing documents, analyzing images, generating images, and running code. Fast response modes make it quick for everyday queries, and a canvas supports working on documents and code beside the chat.

Further features address more advanced needs. Deep research compiles longer reports from web sources, connectors link to services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Notion, and custom agents let users set up specialized assistants. Memory can retain preferences between chats, and mobile apps bring it to phones. The assistant uses Mistral’s own models, some of which are open-weight, and emphasizes European hosting and privacy options.

item.title: Meta AI
item.description: Meta AI is the assistant that Meta put where its users already are. In WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and Facebook, you can mention it in a chat or open it from the search bar to ask a question, get recommendations, or generate an image. There is also a standalone app and website with fuller features, including natural voice conversations, image creation and editing, and a feed where people share what they have made.

item.title: Netomi
item.description:
Netomi builds AI agents for customer support. Large brands connect it to their help desks and back-end systems, and the agents answer questions, track orders, process returns, and handle other requests across channels. Where an agent cannot resolve something, it hands off to a person with context.

The platform learns from past tickets and company content, and is built with controls such as guardrails and testing for regulated and high-volume environments. Customers include airlines, retailers, and travel companies that field heavy, repetitive inquiries.

item.title: Observe.AI
item.description:
Observe.AI is built for contact centers that handle huge numbers of customer interactions. Quality teams traditionally review a small sample of calls by hand. Observe.AI transcribes and scores all interactions automatically against a company’s quality and compliance criteria, flags issues such as missed disclosures or poor handling of angry customers, and surfaces trends across thousands of conversations.

It also supports agents during and after the call. Real-time guidance suggests what to say or reminds an agent of a required step, and post-call summaries cut the time spent on notes. Coaching tools turn scores into specific feedback for each agent, and dashboards help supervisors see which skills to work on. The platform has added AI agents that speak with customers directly for routine requests, handing off to humans when needed.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: Perplexity works more like a search engine than a chatbot. You ask a question, it searches the web in real time, and it writes a short answer with numbered citations you can click to check. That makes it good for current events, product comparisons, and fact-finding where you need to see where the information came from. Follow-up questions keep the context, and you can narrow searches to sources like academic papers or forums.

item.title: Pi
item.description:
Pi was built to be a kind and curious conversational partner instead of a productivity tool. Its responses are short, warm, and conversational, and it often asks follow-up questions, which made it a favorite with people who wanted to talk through ideas, plans, or feelings in a low-pressure setting. It supports voice conversations with several voices, which suits casual use.

Inflection AI, founded by former DeepMind and LinkedIn leaders, launched Pi with the aim of making a personal AI. The company later saw its founders and much of its team join Microsoft, and it pivoted to licensing its models to enterprises. Pi remains online as a free consumer product at pi.ai and in apps, but active development has slowed, and the messaging integrations it once had are gone.

item.title: Poe
item.description:
Poe gives access to many AI models without separate accounts. A single app and website lets you switch between leading chatbots, image generators, and video tools, compare answers, and keep your conversations in one place. This is helpful for people who want to try different models and use whichever works best for each task.

Creators can build bots on top of models with custom prompts and knowledge, and publish them for others, with ways to earn revenue based on usage. The platform also offers an app builder and an API so developers can use Poe’s models in their projects. Group chats let multiple bots and people interact in one conversation.

item.title: Replika
item.description: Replika is one of the earliest AI companion apps. You create an avatar, choose a name and appearance, and begin chatting. Over time the AI builds a memory of your interests, relationships, and preferences, and the avatar responds in a way that reflects that history. Users talk to it about their day, vent about problems, practice conversations, or just keep company. It offers text chat, voice calls, and an augmented reality mode that places the avatar in your room.

item.title: Siri
item.description: Siri is the assistant that comes with every Apple device. You say “Hey Siri” or hold a button, then ask it to send a message, set a timer, call someone, play music, adjust a setting, or control HomeKit devices. It works across Apple’s hardware, so the same assistant is on your wrist, in your car through CarPlay, and on a smart speaker. Its biggest advantage is how deeply it ties into the system, since it can act on messages, calendars, reminders, and photos without extra setup.

item.title: Talkdesk
item.description:
Talkdesk provides the software contact centers use to handle calls and messages. Customers reach an agent by phone, chat, or messaging, and the platform routes them, records interactions, and reports on performance. Cloud delivery makes setup quicker than legacy systems.

AI is part of each layer. Virtual agents resolve common requests, agent assist suggests replies and surfaces knowledge during calls, quality tools score conversations automatically, and forecasting helps schedule staff. Industry versions serve healthcare, financial services, and retail.

item.title: Venice AI
item.description: Venice AI builds its pitch around privacy and freedom of use. The company states it does not log or store conversations on its servers, and that chats are kept in the user’s browser, which appeals to people uneasy about their prompts being retained or used for training. It runs open-source models, so users can pick from several language models and an image generator, and the platform applies fewer content restrictions than many mainstream services.

item.title: Zendesk
item.description:
Zendesk is one of the most widely used help desk systems. Customer messages from email, web chat, phone, WhatsApp, and social media become tickets in a shared workspace, where they can be routed, prioritized, and tracked against service targets. A help center and community forum let customers find answers themselves, and reports show response times and satisfaction. It scales from small support teams to large contact centers.

The current product is built around AI. AI agents take on requests from start to finish, answering from help articles and past conversations, and taking actions in connected systems when allowed. A copilot assists human agents by suggesting replies, summarizing long threads, and flagging urgent or unhappy customers. The platform has added contact center, workforce management, and quality assurance tools, and an employee service product that applies the same ideas to internal IT and HR requests.

item.title: Zowie
item.description:
Zowie focuses on online retail support. Its AI agent connects to a store’s order system, answers questions about delivery and returns, processes simple actions, and hands off tricky cases to staff. It works across chat, email, and messaging channels.

The platform emphasizes decision-making that follows a brand’s policies, and gives support managers tools to review and adjust behavior. Analytics show resolution rates and topics.

Zowie is sold on subscription. Alternatives include Gorgias, Intercom Fin, Ada, Netomi, and Zendesk AI agents. Zowie suits e-commerce support teams.

item.title: Aisera
item.description: Aisera provides AI agents for internal and external service desks. Employees can ask for help with IT issues, such as resetting a password or requesting software, or HR questions, such as time off policies, and the agent resolves the request by taking actions in connected systems instead of simply pointing to articles. For customers, similar agents handle support inquiries. The goal is to reduce the number of tickets that reach human staff.

item.title: Alexa AI
item.description:
Alexa popularized the smart speaker. You speak to an Echo device to play music, set timers, control lights, check weather, shop on Amazon, and ask questions. Over the years, it grew into a platform with thousands of skills from third parties and support for a huge range of smart home devices. It’s built into many speakers, TVs, cars, and appliances.

Alexa+ is the next generation. Built on large language models, including Amazon’s own Nova and models from other providers, it holds more natural conversations, understands context across a dialogue, and can handle multi-step requests such as planning an evening, booking a reservation, or coordinating a family calendar. It can act across services, remember preferences, and work with smart home devices more flexibly, and a web and app experience complements the voice interface. Some promised features arrived later than first shown.

item.title: Front
item.description:
Front treats shared inboxes like collaborative workspaces. Support, sales, and account teams manage messages from several channels in one place, assign conversations, leave internal comments, and see who is handling what. The interface resembles email, so adoption is easy.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules route messages, tag them, and set priorities, while AI summarizes long threads, suggests replies, and answers common questions. Analytics show response times and workloads, and integrations with CRMs and helpdesk tools provide context.

item.title: Mavenoid
item.description:
Mavenoid focuses on products people have trouble setting up or fixing. Instead of a long manual or a phone queue, customers use an interactive guide that asks questions, narrows down the problem, and walks through steps with pictures and videos. If the guide cannot solve it, it hands off to support with the details collected.

Manufacturers build these flows from their manuals and support data, and AI helps generate and maintain content, answer free-text questions, and spot recurring issues. Analytics show where customers get stuck, which feeds back to product teams.

item.title: Sapling
item.description:
Sapling helps support and sales teams write faster and more consistently. As an agent types in the help desk or CRM, Sapling suggests completions based on past replies, fixes grammar and tone, and inserts approved snippets. This reduces typing time and variation.

Managers use quality analytics to monitor response times and consistency, and see how suggestions are used. It integrates with Zendesk, Salesforce, Intercom, and other tools, and offers an API and an AI content detector.

item.title: Anna
item.description:
Anna presents itself as an adaptive AI companion. Instead of treating every chat as new, it tries to remember what you have told it and adjusts its tone and suggestions as it learns your preferences and goals. That continuity is the main selling point of companion-style apps.

People use apps like this for conversation, motivation, planning, and reflection. They differ from task-focused assistants in that they emphasize an ongoing relationship. Mainstream assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have also added memory, so the line between categories is blurring.

item.title: Chai
item.description:
Chai lets people talk to a huge variety of AI personalities. Users browse or search for characters, such as a friendly companion, a fantasy hero, or a fictional figure, and chat in a messaging-style interface. Creators can build their own characters by writing a short description and a first message, and they are shared with the community, which has produced a very large catalog.

The experience is aimed at entertainment and companionship. The AI maintains a persona and some memory of the conversation, and the app offers features such as voice and image options and a feed of popular bots. Free users see ads and message limits, while subscribers get faster responses and more features.

item.title: Character.ai
item.description: Character.AI lets you chat with an enormous catalog of AI personalities. Some are based on fictional characters or historical figures, many are invented by users, and you can build your own by writing a description of who the character is and how they talk. The results feel more like acting than answering questions: the characters stay in persona, remember what you have said in the conversation, and respond in a distinctive voice. Users spend long sessions on it, using it for role-play, story writing, language practice, and casual company.

item.title: ChatPlayground AI
item.description:
ChatPlayground addresses a simple question: which model is best for this task? Instead of opening several chatbots in separate tabs, a user types a prompt once and sees answers from multiple models side by side, including offerings from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and open models.

That helps with writing, coding, and research tasks where quality varies by model. Users can save conversations, keep prompts organized, and switch between models while working. For people who pay for several subscriptions, a single place can be convenient.

item.title: Drift
item.description: Drift popularized the idea of replacing a website contact form with a live conversation. A chat widget greets visitors, asks a few questions, and either answers them, routes them to the right salesperson, or books a meeting on the spot. For B2B companies with long sales cycles, the goal was to catch interested visitors while they were still on the site instead of waiting for them to fill out a form and wait for a reply.

item.title: Grok
item.description: Grok is the chatbot from xAI, Elon Musk’s AI company. It is built into X, so you can ask it about a post, a trending topic, or a thread without leaving the feed, and it is also available as a separate app and at grok.com. Its main distinguishing feature is live access to posts on X, which makes it unusually quick at summarizing what people are saying about a breaking story. The tone is a little looser than other assistants, and it will answer some questions that more cautious tools decline.

item.title: Kin Personal AI
item.description:
Kin positions itself as a private personal AI. Users talk with an assistant that remembers their circumstances and offers guidance across areas of life, with specialized advisors that focus on different topics. The conversation builds a profile over time so advice reflects what the user has shared.

Privacy is the main selling point. The company states that personal data is stored locally on the device and encrypted, rather than in a central cloud, so sensitive details are less exposed. This appeals to people who want to discuss personal matters without handing data to a large platform.

item.title: Kindroid
item.description:
Kindroid lets users create a companion from scratch. You write the character’s background and personality, choose how they look using generated images, and give them a voice, and then talk by text or voice calls. The app emphasizes memory, so the character can recall details from earlier conversations, and users can adjust how the AI responds by editing the character’s profile and diary.

Other features include group chats with several characters, image generation of the character in various scenes, and selfie sharing. Users value the high level of control and the more natural conversation compared with simpler chatbots. Some use it for roleplay and storytelling, others for companionship or practicing conversation.

item.title: Littlebird
item.description:
Littlebird tries to understand what you are working on. It observes activity across apps, such as messages, meetings, documents, and web pages, and builds a memory of context. When a user asks for help, such as summarizing a project status or drafting a reply, it draws on that history.

The pitch is an assistant that does not need to be told everything each time. That convenience comes with a privacy tradeoff, since an always-on tool sees a lot of work content. Users should understand what is captured, where it is stored, and how to pause or delete it.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot
item.description: Microsoft uses the Copilot name for a family of assistants rather than one product. The consumer Copilot app and website work like other AI chatbots: you can ask questions, generate text and images, talk by voice, and have it look at your screen or camera for help with what you are doing. It is built into Windows and the Edge browser, where it can summarize pages, compare information across open tabs, and help with tasks as you browse.

item.title: Notis
item.description:
Notis works where people already chat. Users send a text or voice note to the assistant in a messaging app, and it can save notes, draft emails, set tasks, search the web, or update tools like Notion and calendars. The aim is to reduce the friction of opening several apps.

Connections to services such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Notion let the assistant act on requests, and it keeps a memory of preferences. Voice notes are transcribed and organized.

item.title: TheLibrarian.io
item.description:
TheLibrarian.io puts an assistant in WhatsApp. Users message it to check their email, schedule events, create tasks, and get reminders, in natural language or voice notes. It connects to services like Gmail and Google Calendar.

The appeal is simplicity: no new interface, and the chat is available anywhere. Connecting an assistant to email and calendars requires trust, so review permissions and privacy terms.

Independent information is limited. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Notis, Poke, Lindy, Motion, and ChatGPT with connectors. TheLibrarian.io suits people who want to manage tasks through WhatsApp.

item.title: Tidio
item.description:
Tidio targets small online businesses that want to answer customers quickly without a big support team. A chat widget on the website lets visitors ask questions, and the tool collects messages from chat, email, and social channels in one inbox. Visual chatbot flows handle common tasks, such as collecting contact details, recommending products, and recovering abandoned carts.

Lyro, its AI agent, answers customer questions using the store’s help content and product data, and hands off to a human when needed. Automations trigger messages based on visitor behavior, and integrations with Shopify, WordPress, WooCommerce, and others bring in order and product information. Tidio is aimed at ease of setup, and most stores can install it in minutes.

item.title: Watermelon
item.description:
Watermelon is aimed at support teams that want automation without engineering. They design conversation flows in a visual builder, train the bot on help content, and connect it to chat channels such as websites and WhatsApp. Complex cases transfer to humans with the conversation history.

AI features answer free-form questions from a knowledge base, and analytics show resolution rates and topics. The platform includes a shared inbox for agents, so the bot and humans work in one system.
